Subtitle EN: On Labour and the Human Cost of Artificial Intelligence
Web Preview Text EN: I’d prefer not to is an interactive installation exposing the labour given by humans to train machines, reversing the present mythological representation of machines working for humans. It uses CAPTCHAs in an attempt to unveil part of the labour hidden behind everyday online actions.
Description EN:
I’d prefer not to is an interactive installation exploring the hidden labor that trains AI. On small screens, visitors interact with stations built from image and text CAPTCHAs (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart), addressing themes such as click work, data labeling, image annotation and behavioural monitoring. The CAPTCHA becomes a metaphor for this inverted division of labour: its limited character space imposes constraints, yet enables an abstract, almost poetic narrative that remains recognisable.
The aesthetic references “click farms”—coordinated activity by low-paid workers or bots, generating fake online interactions like ad clicks, video views and social media “likes”. And this in circumstances more amenable to computing devices than to humans.

The project engages with debates on AI governance, platform work and data rights. Reversing the idea that AI replaces human labor, it shows how AI systems are painstakingly trained, corrected and maintained by millions of largely invisible, poorly paid or unpaid people, confronting visitors with their own unconscious involvement in data production.

I’d prefer not to is made by Bernadette Geiger (BE), Félicien Goguey (CH/FR) and Hans Lammerant (BE), with Marta Revuelta (CH/ES) as contributor. The project is one of the seven installations produced in CODE 2026, a co-creation project on digital agency. CODE is organized by IMPAKT (NL) in collaboration with Werktank (BE), Privacy Salon / CPDP (BE) and In Fine (CH).
Web Preview Text DE: I’d prefer not to macht die menschliche Arbeit, mit der Maschinen trainiert werden sichtbar, und kehrt damit den Mythos um, demzufolge Maschinen für Menschen arbeiten würden. Das Projekt nutzt CAPTCHAs, um die Arbeit aufzudecken, die sich hinter alltäglichen Online-Handlungen verbirgt.
Description DE:
I'd prefer not to ist eine interaktive Installation, die sich mit der unsichtbaren Arbeit beschäftigt, die zum Trainieren von KI aufgewendet wird. An kleinen Bildschirmen interagieren Besucher*innen mit Stationen, die aus Bild- und Text-CAPTCHAs (“Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart”) aufgebaut sind, und setzen sich dabei mit Themen wie Klickarbeit, Data Labeling, Bildannotation und Verhaltensüberwachung auseinander. Das CAPTCHA wird dabei zur Metapher für diese umgekehrte Arbeitsteilung: Der begrenzte Platz für Zeichen schränkt zwar ein, ermöglicht jedoch zugleich eine abstrakte, beinahe poetische Erzählung mit Wiedererkennungswert. Die Ästhetik bezieht sich auf “Click Farms” – koordinierte Tätigkeiten von schlecht bezahlten Arbeiter*innen oder Bots, die gefälschte Online-Interaktionen wie Werbeklicks, Videoaufrufe und Social-Media-”Likes” erzeugen.

Das Projekt beteiligt sich an Debatten über KI-Governance, Plattformarbeit und Datenrechte. Es kehrt die Vorstellung um, KI ersetze menschliche Arbeit, und zeigt stattdessen, wie KI-Systeme mühsam von Millionen weitgehend unsichtbarer, schlecht oder gar nicht bezahlter Menschen trainiert, korrigiert und gewartet werden. Dadurch werden Besucher*innen mit ihrer eigenen unbewussten Beteiligung an der Produktion von Daten konfrontiert.

I'd prefer not to wurde von Bernadette Geiger (BE), Félicien Goguey (CH/FR) und Hans Lammerant (BE) realisiert, mit Marta Revuelta (CH/ES) als Mitwirkende. Das Projekt ist eine von sieben Installationen, die im Rahmen von CODE 2026 entstanden sind, einem Co-Creation-Projekt zu digitaler Agency. CODE wird von IMPAKT (NL) in Zusammenarbeit mit Werktank (BE), Privacy Salon / CPDP (BE) und In Fine (CH) organisiert.

Name EN: Negotiating Reality – Conflict Culture,  AI and Democracy in the Digital Public Sphere
Web Preview Text EN: This conference takes Negotiating Humanity as its starting point to explore how democratic discourse can be strengthened in increasingly complex digital information ecosystems.
Description EN:
Democracy has always depended on places where different perspectives can meet, disagreement can be negotiated and shared futures can be imagined. Today, many of these encounters take place online, in digital spaces shaped by the logics of attention, amplification and emotional engagement. Here, disagreement can easily turn into polarization and fragmentation, while disinformation is increasingly used to deepen social divides, undermine trust and advance geopolitical interests.
This conference takes Negotiating Humanity as its starting point to explore how democratic discourse can be strengthened in increasingly complex digital information ecosystems.
The programme looks at the forces transforming the digital public sphere—from platform architectures and algorithmic amplification to information manipulation and the psychological dynamics behind polarization. Through current examples, it examines how conflicts are intensified, how disinformation and AI-generated content are changing the information landscape and what these developments reveal about the changing conditions of democratic life.
But the conference does not stop at diagnosis. The second part turns towards the possibilities ahead. If digital spaces have become an important part of our public life, how might we shape them to better support democratic participation and constructive disagreement? What new forms of digital inclusion, deliberation and civic participation could emerge? And how might AI contribute to these processes—not only as a technology that needs to be governed, but as a tool for building new democratic infrastructures?
Together, we will look at the digital spaces of the future and consider how to make them places where democracy can not only survive, but evolve.

Name EN: A Cartography of Genocide: Israel’s Conduct in Gaza Since October 2023
Web Preview Text EN: Forensic Architecture’s monitoring and research consists of an interactive cartographic platform and a text report, which deploy spatial and pattern analysis to observe the ways in which Israel’s military operations entailed widespread civilian harm.
Description EN:
Since the start of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza in October 2023, Forensic Architecture (FA) has collected vast amounts of data related to attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure by the Israeli military, painstakingly documenting the near-total destruction of the conditions of life in Gaza. Their team has collected, verified and analyzed thousands of videos showing individual incidents of atrocities.
An interactive cartographic database and accompanying text report outline the ways in which Israel’s military operations have entailed widespread civilian harm, and identify patterns which indicate a systematic and organized campaign to destroy life, the conditions necessary for life and life-sustaining infrastructure. The web-based cartographic platform is an iterative, live interface which is continually updated. Filtering and cross-referencing functions allow users to explore trends within datasets, illuminating patterns across datasets and relationships between individual incidents.
Vital stories are revealed through this research. Evacuation orders issued by the Israeli military have resulted in the repeated large-scale displacement of the Palestinian population across Gaza, often to areas which are insufficiently prepared to sustain the lives of hundreds of thousands of displaced people, and which, despite being designated as “safe”, have subsequently come under military attack. Israel’s attempts to criminalize and kill medical staff and destroy their sites of operation has made both seeking and providing medical care in Gaza an unprecedentedly dangerous venture, driving further displacement. Meanwhile, the “ceasefire” of October 2025 is, in practice, a ceasefire in name only, as the project reveals the continued systematic destruction of neighborhoods, camps and cities, along with continued attacks on Palestinian civilians.
Reports derived from the platform have been submitted numerous times in support of the South African legal team currently bringing a generational genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice in the Hague, while the platform and its findings have also been repeatedly cited by UN Special Rapporteurs and other major international bodies.
Web Preview Text DE: Die umfangreiche Recherche von Forensic Architecture setzt sich damit auseinander, in welcher Weise die israelischen Militäroperationen weitreichenden Schaden an der Zivilbevölkerung verursacht haben.
Description DE:
Seit Beginn der israelischen Militäroperation im Gazastreifen im Oktober 2023 hat Forensic Architecture (FA) umfangreiche Daten zu Angriffen des israelischen Militärs auf Zivilist*innen und zivile Infrastruktur gesammelt und dabei akribisch die nahezu vollständige Zerstörung der Lebensgrundlagen im Gazastreifen dokumentiert. Das Team hat Tausende von Videos gesammelt, verifiziert und analysiert, die einzelne Vorfälle von Gräueltaten zeigen. Eine interaktive kartografische Datenbank sowie ein begleitender Bericht zeigen auf, in welcher Weise Israels Militäroperationen weitreichende Schäden für die Zivilbevölkerung verursacht haben. Sie identifizieren Muster, die auf eine systematische und organisierte Kampagne zur Zerstörung von Leben, der für das Leben notwendigen Bedingungen und lebenserhaltender Infrastruktur hindeuten. Die webbasierte kartografische Plattform ist eine iterative Live-Schnittstelle, die kontinuierlich aktualisiert wird. Filter- und Querverweisfunktionen ermöglichen es Nutzer*innen, Trends innerhalb der Datensätze zu erkunden, wodurch Muster zwischen verschiedenen Datensätzen sowie Zusammenhänge zwischen einzelnen Vorfällen sichtbar werden.
Diese Recherche bringt zentrale Erkenntnisse ans Licht. Evakuierungsanordnungen des israelischen Militärs haben wiederholt zur großflächigen Vertreibung der palästinensischen Bevölkerung im gesamten Gazastreifen geführt – oft in Gebiete, die nicht ausreichend darauf vorbereitet sind, das Leben Hunderttausender Vertriebener zu sichern, und die, obwohl als “sicher” ausgewiesen, in der Folge selbst zu militärischen Angriffszielen wurden. Israels Versuche, medizinisches Personal zu kriminalisieren und zu töten sowie deren Einsatzorte zu zerstören, haben sowohl die Inanspruchnahme als auch die Bereitstellung medizinischer Versorgung im Gazastreifen zu einem beispiellos gefährlichen Unterfangen gemacht und damit weitere Vertreibung vorangetrieben. Die “Waffenruhe” vom Oktober 2025 ist in der Praxis nur dem Namen nach eine Waffenruhe, wie das Projekt zeigt: Die systematische Zerstörung von Wohnvierteln, Lagern und Städten setzt sich ebenso fort wie die Angriffe auf palästinensische Zivilpersonen.
Die aus der Plattform hervorgegangenen Berichte wurden wiederholt zur Unterstützung des südafrikanischen Rechtsteams eingereicht, das derzeit vor dem Internationalen Gerichtshof in Den Haag ein Verfahren wegen Völkermords gegen Israel führt. Zudem wurden die Plattform und ihre Ergebnisse wiederholt von UN-Sonderberichterstatter*innen und anderen bedeutenden internationalen Organisationen zitiert.

National Gallery Dreaming is an Al-powered interactive installation that explores the hidden relationships within the National Gallery, London’s collection. Developed in collaboration with digital agency Numiko as part of the Gallery’s NGX innovation program, this audio-visual project combines computer vision, collection metadata, generative soundscapes by composer and sound artist Ben Eyes and knowledge graph technologies to uncover connections between artworks, artists, places, people, ideas and the viewer. As it responds National Gallery Dreaming reveals unexpected pathways through more than 2,400 artworks, creating a dynamic visualization of the collection’s rich interconnectedness. By making its reasoning visible and drawing on the expertise embedded in the Gallery’s collection data, the project demonstrates how Al can offer new ways of discovering and interpreting art while deepening public engagement with cultural collections.

Name EN: Democracy in the Age of Digital Polarization
Web Preview Text EN: In Isaac Asimov’s 1955 story Franchise, future America is still a democracy, but a strange one: parties and candidates campaign for office but citizens have been freed of the burden of voting. A supercomputer, gently named Multivac, can very nearly compute how every American would vote.
Description EN:
In Isaac Asimov’s 1955 story Franchise, future America is still a democracy, but a strange one: parties and candidates campaign for office but citizens have been freed of the burden of voting. A supercomputer, gently named Multivac, can very nearly compute how every American would vote. And on the election day the machine selects the single citizen who will be the Voter of the Year. He is not asked whom he prefers. He is asked how he feels about the price of eggs and other ordinary questions. After the machine has measured the emotional intensity of his answers, the winners of every contest in the nation, from the presidency to the county board, are announced. No one else votes. No one needs to.

Asimov’s America has solved the problem that has haunted democracy since its birth: its divisiveness. This is a democracy without a majority and a minority. There are no celebrating crowds in the streets on election night, and no defeated ones. Nobody knows how many black Americans or union households or college-educated women elected the president, because nothing was counted; nobody may abstain, since the preferences of all are consulted and the votes of none.

Asimov understood what he was abolishing. His founding fathers feared the public counting of votes because counting is how democracy manufactures losers—and losers, shown precisely how outnumbered they are, do not always accept arithmetic as a verdict. Every election is a civil war prevented by bookkeeping; the perpetual danger is that the count loses its authority—that the sight of their opponents’ numerical superiority no longer binds the defeated, who withdraw their consent. But is Asimov’s Franchise the desired alternative of our democracies polarized by Multivac’s grandchildren?

Name EN: From Outrage to Influence: How Psychology, Creators and Platforms Shape Political Debate
Artists: Isabel Linzer (US), Jon Roozenbeek (NL/GB), Alexander Sängerlaub (DE)
Web Preview Text EN: Why does outrage spread so easily online—and how does it turn into political influence? This conversation brings together psychological insights and a closer look at the growing influence of social media creators in shaping political debate.
Description EN:
Why does outrage spread so easily online—and how does it turn into political influence? This conversation brings together psychological insights and a closer look at the growing influence of social media creators in shaping political debate.

Jon Roozenbeek explores the psychological and social mechanisms that make people respond to conflict, outrage and group identities, and how digital environments can amplify these tendencies. He looks at why polarization persists and what happens when human psychology meets platforms built around attention and engagement.

Isabel Linzer turns to the rise of political content creators, who increasingly move between the roles of journalist, activist, campaign proxy, advertiser or everyday influencer. As political organizations work with creators to reach specific communities through voices their audiences already trust, creators have become an increasingly important source of political information. But this growing influence also raises key democratic questions around election integrity, free expression, transparency and covert influence.

Moderated by Alexander Sängerlaub, the conversation brings these perspectives together to examine how psychology, platform dynamics and the creator economy interact—and what it would take to create digital spaces where political influence can strengthen democratic debate rather than feed polarization.

Name EN: Weaponized Information - Disinformation as a Geopolitical Tool
Artists: Gustav Gressel (AT/DE), Jan Nicola Beyer (DE), Jessikka Aro (FI), Masha Borzunova (DE)
Web Preview Text EN: Disinformation is no longer simply a problem of false information. It has become a tool of geopolitical influence—used to exploit existing tensions, shape public narratives and undermine trust in democratic institutions.
Description EN:
Disinformation is no longer simply a problem of false information. It has become a tool of geopolitical influence—used to exploit existing tensions, shape public narratives and undermine trust in democratic institutions. As AI makes it easier to produce and distribute convincing content at scale, the information space itself is becoming a field of conflict.

This panel brings together perspectives from security and geopolitical analysis, investigative journalism and the practical fight against information manipulation. Drawing on experience with Russian propaganda and influence operations, the participants examine how coordinated disinformation campaigns work, how they target societies and how they shape the environment in which journalists, institutions and citizens operate.

The discussion also considers how journalists and platforms can respond without inadvertently amplifying manipulation and how democracies can defend themselves while protecting freedom of expression and open public debate.

Rather than treating disinformation as a problem that can simply be fact-checked away, the panel explores the wider infrastructures and strategies behind information warfare—and considers what democratic resilience could look like in an information environment where the boundaries between communication, manipulation and political influence are increasingly difficult to draw.

Name EN: Designing for Peace: Technology, Trust and the Future of How We Live Together
Web Preview Text EN: Every day, we hear about AI getting better at doing human tasks. But are those capabilities making us humans better or worse at living together in peace? This keynote will point to emerging evidence and a fast-moving frontier of experimentation by technologists and peacebuilders across the world.
Description EN:
Every day, we hear about AI getting better at doing human tasks. But are those capabilities making us humans better or worse at living together in peace?
What if we evaluated AI through a different lens: its effect on our capacity to coexist? Our ability to navigate disagreement. To live with diversity and difference. To build relationships grounded in trust, dignity and belonging.
This keynote will point to emerging evidence and a fast-moving frontier of experimentation by technologists and peacebuilders across the world: listening and sensemaking at scale, AI-supported deliberation, AI coaching for constructive disagreement and new forms of collective decision-making.
But the promise comes with peril. Conversational AI is often designed to be frictionless, agreeable and even sycophantic. As our reliance on it grows, do we risk flattening difference, obscuring the limits of what AI knows, or dulling our own capacity to disagree, deliberate and make sense of the world together?
The race to build more capable AI is already underway. The deeper challenge is whether those capabilities can help us build a more peaceful world.
Funding Line: Presented in the context of fAIr media. fAIr media is co-funded by the Creative Europe programme of the European Union under grant agreement 101147977.

Name EN: Designing the Digital Public: Building Spaces for Democratic Negotiation
Artists: Jaya Klara Brekke (SE/GB), Harry Keller (DE), Lena Slachmuijlder (BE), Lucas Evers (NL), Mushon Zer-Aviv (IL/CH)
Web Preview Text EN: What if we stopped asking how democracy can adapt to the digital spaces we already have—and started designing those spaces with democracy in mind?
Description EN:
What if we stopped asking how democracy can adapt to the digital spaces we already have—and started designing those spaces with democracy in mind?

The final session of the conference turns from diagnosis to possibility, inviting the speakers to imagine the digital institutions and public spaces of the future. If digital environments have become places where we meet, exchange ideas, form opinions and negotiate social conflicts, they also need to support the democratic processes that make living together possible.

The discussion explores what it could mean to design digital spaces for democratic negotiation: spaces where people can encounter perspectives different from their own, stay engaged through disagreement and take part in shaping decisions that affect their communities. It considers which democratic functions such spaces should fulfil, who should be responsible for designing and governing them and how technologies such as AI could support dialogue and deliberation rather than reinforce polarization.

The session closes the conference by moving from understanding the digital public sphere we have today to imagining the one we want to build: what kinds of digital institutions could help societies negotiate difference, remain connected across disagreement and create new spaces for democratic life?

Description EN: While tech-billionaires publicly celebrate their ”techno-optimism” (Andreessen), they secretly prepare for the possible consequences of their disruptive actions. In face of scenarios like climate collapse or civil wars they seek safety in private luxury bunkers, space colonies or in uploading their minds to the cloud; pursuing private exit-strategies rather than using their vast resources to make the world a better place. How did we get from the possibilities of the early cyber utopias to the catastrophising fantasies of the tech bros—and how can we reactivate a commitment to the interdependent ”Team Human”? Web Preview Text EN: Dehumanization rarely begins with violence. It begins with language, with images, with enemy stereotypes in everyday life. This conference program asks how patterns of dehumanization work, and what art, culture and institutions can set against them.
Description EN:
Dehumanization rarely begins with violence. It begins with language, with images, with enemy stereotypes in everyday life. Antisemitism is one of the oldest patterns of this kind, and in the digital space it is simultaneously taking on new, accelerated forms: algorithms amplify outrage and enemy images, antisemitic narratives spread globally and instantly, old stereotypes resurface in new digital forms and threats born online increasingly spill into physical, everyday life. When words become weapons and language itself becomes the site of conflict, the question arises: Who sets the conditions under which we take positions and who has the right to name them?

The Ars Electronica Festival understands itself as an infrastructure for negotiation, a space in which moral certainties can once again become open questions and in which conflicts are not resolved, but made workable. Conflict competence is not an abstract virtue here, but a fundamental condition of democracy. This conference is one such space. It asks how patterns of dehumanization work and what art, culture and institutions can set against them.

Yehuda Cohen, Emmanuel Witzthum, Zuhdi Najeeb, Luc Bernard, Emilie Moatti and Daphna Horenczyk come from very different fields: political journalism, literature, a shared Israeli-Palestinian cultural center in Jerusalem and digital game development that uses media for Holocaust education and against antisemitism. Together, they take on a subject with no easy answers—one that needs, above all, a space in which those answers can be discussed.

Web Preview Text DE: Entmenschlichung beginnt selten mit Gewalt. Sie beginnt mit Sprache, mit Stereotypen, mit Feindbildern im Alltag. Das Konferenzprogramm Patterns of Dehumanization fragt, wie Systeme der Entmenschlichung funktionieren und was Kunst, Kultur und Institutionen ihnen entgegensetzen können.
Description DE:
Entmenschlichung beginnt selten mit Gewalt. Sie beginnt mit Sprache, mit Bildern, mit Feindbildern im Alltag. Antisemitismus ist eines der ältesten Muster dieser Art und nimmt im digitalen Raum zugleich neue, beschleunigte Formen an: Algorithmen verstärken Empörung und Feindbilder, antisemitische Narrative verbreiten sich global und unmittelbar, alte Stereotype tauchen in neuen digitalen Formen wieder auf, und Bedrohungen, die online entstehen, wirken zunehmend in das physische Alltagsleben hinein. Wenn Begriffe zu Waffen und Sprache selbst zum Ort des Konflikts werden, stellt sich die Frage, wer die Bedingungen setzt, unter denen wir Positionen einnehmen und wer das Recht hat, diese zu benennen. 

Das Ars Electronica Festival versteht sich als Infrastruktur des Verhandelns, als ein Raum, in dem moralische Gewissheiten wieder zur Frage werden können und in dem Konflikte nicht aufgehoben, sondern bearbeitbar gemacht werden. Konfliktfähigkeit ist dabei keine abstrakte Tugend, sondern eine demokratische Grundbedingung. Das Konferenzprogramm Patterns of Dehumanization ist ein solcher Raum: Es fragt, wie Systeme der Entmenschlichung funktionieren und was Kunst, Kultur und Institutionen ihnen entgegensetzen können. 

Yehuda Cohen, Emmanuel Witzthum, Zuhdi Najeeb, Luc Bernard, Emilie Moatti und Daphna Horenczyk bringen dabei sehr unterschiedliche Perspektiven mit: aus der politischen Publizistik, aus der Literatur, aus einem geteilten israelisch-palästinensischen Kulturhaus in Jerusalem und aus der digitalen Spieleentwicklung, wo Bernard digitale Medien zur Holocaust-Bildung und gegen Antisemitismus in der Gaming-Industrie einsetzt. Gemeinsam widmen sie sich einem Thema, das keine einfachen Antworten kennt, aber einen Raum braucht, in dem diese verhandelt werden können.

Name EN: Practicing Impact: When Reality Talks Back
Web Preview Text EN: Ideas are easy. The real work begins when they meet reality—and other people. Join the Ars Electronica Futurelab and various collaborators for an open Town Hall exploring what it takes to turn ideas into reality, and what reality teaches us in return.
Description EN: The Ars Electronica Futurelab explores the future by building it—together with companies, institutions, researchers, artists, designers and the public. This Town Hall brings together collaborators who turn ideas into reality. When existing formats no longer fit, we invent new ones. Rather than presenting success stories, we share the realities of experimentation, negotiation and practice—because impact is not an idea. It is something you create by doing.
Web Preview Text DE: Ideen zu entwickeln ist einfach. Die eigentliche Arbeit beginnt, wenn sie auf die Realität treffen – und auf andere Menschen. Nimm gemeinsam mit dem Ars Electronica Futurelab und seinen Partner*innen an einer offenen Diskussion teil: Wir erörtern, was nötig ist, um Ideen in die Realität umzusetzen, und was uns die Realität im Gegenzug lehrt.
Description DE: Das Ars Electronica Futurelab erforscht die Zukunft, indem es sie gestaltet – gemeinsam mit Unternehmen, Institutionen, Forschenden, Künstler*innen, Designer*innen und der Öffentlichkeit. Dieses Town Hall-Event bringt Partner*innen zusammen, die Ideen in die Realität umsetzen. Wenn bestehende Formate nicht mehr passen, erfinden wir neue. Anstatt Erfolgsgeschichten zu präsentieren, teilen wir die Realitäten des Experimentierens, der Verhandlung und der Praxis – denn Wirkung ist keine Idee. Sie entsteht durch Handeln.

Web Preview Text EN: What happens when a machine mixes paintings without any text prompts? Fluidity of Images explores the juxtaposition space between images, where two images combine to reveal a spectrum of new visual forms, condensations and compositions.
Description EN:
What happens when a machine mixes paintings without text prompts? Fluidity of Images explores the juxtaposition space between images: the territory between two source works where they combine to different extents to reveal a spectrum of new forms, condensations and compositions. It situates this practice within a broader continuum of procedural and collective artistic practices, where agency is distributed across processes, tools and collaborators.

Subtitle EN: A hands-on session on how music changes what a work means.
Web Preview Text EN: Who decides the music when machines generate endless sound on demand? Read a scene to music and hear that same moment take on three different directions. Then see how CORPUS lets the musicians who make the music have co-ownership over it. Filmmakers, game designers and musicians can all take part.
Description EN: This workshop asks who decides the music when machines generate endless sound on demand, which is as much a cultural question as it is an artistic one. Participants read a scene to music and then hear that same moment take on three different directions by using Soundbook, a tool built by Mathis Nitschke’s EU co-funded CORPUS project at Sofilab. He then demonstrates how contributing musicians actually co-own this corpus of music as opposed to simply supplying it. Filmmakers, game designers and musicians can all take part.
Additional Info EN: For musicians, composers and producers, and for people on the visual and audiovisual side: visual artists, filmmakers, game designers, and anyone building interactive experiences. The shared question is what music does to a work, so no prior technical knowledge is needed. Participants who want to follow the software part should bring their own laptop or iPad; a stable WiFi connection is required. The session plays music and audio examples over speakers.

Web Preview Text EN: What if AI didn’t give answers, but helped people have better conversations? Water Whisperer is an immersive installation where visitors encounter the voices of different waters and collectively explore the challenges, values, and futures of life with water.
Description EN: Water Whisperer explores how AI can facilitate collective dialogue while inviting visitors to experience water not as a resource to be managed, but as a living ecology of interconnected voices. Inside an immersive pneumatic environment, participants encounter the perspectives of the Danube, groundwater, wastewater, rain, fog and snow. Rather than providing answers, the AI encourages discussion, negotiation and collective reflection on questions surrounding climate adaptation and urban futures. By shifting the conversation from a human-centered perspective toward an ecological one, visitors are invited to recognize themselves as participants within the water cycle rather than observers of it. The installation proposes a new role for AI: not as a technology that replaces human judgment, but as a facilitator of dialogue that helps people listen, exchange perspectives and imagine shared futures. Each session concludes with a speculative postcard co-created from the group’s conversation.
Web Preview Text DE: Was wäre, wenn KI nicht einfach Antworten liefern würde, sondern Menschen dabei helfen könnte, bessere Gespräche zu führen? In Water Whisperer begegnen Besucher*innen den Stimmen unterschiedlicher Gewässer und erkunden die Herausforderungen, Werte und Zukunftsperspektiven des Lebens mit Wasser.
Description DE: Water Whisperer untersucht, wie KI kollektive Dialoge unterstützen kann, und lädt Besucher*innen dazu ein, Wasser nicht als zu verwaltende Ressource, sondern als lebendige Ökologie miteinander verbundener Stimmen zu erleben. In einer immersiven, pneumatischen Umgebung begegnen die Teilnehmenden den Perspektiven von Donau, Grundwasser, Abwasser, Regen, Nebel und Schnee. Anstatt Antworten zu liefern, regt die KI zu Diskussion, Verhandlung und gemeinsamer Reflexion über Fragen der Klimaanpassung und urbaner Zukünfte an. Indem der Blick von einer menschzentrierten hin zu einer ökologischen Perspektive verschoben wird, erfahren sich die Besucher*innen selbst als Teil des Wasserkreislaufs statt als bloße Beobachter*innen. Die Installation entwirft damit eine neue Rolle für KI: nicht als Technologie, die menschliches Urteilsvermögen ersetzt, sondern als Ermöglicherin eines Dialogs, der Menschen hilft zuzuhören, Perspektiven auszutauschen und gemeinsame Zukünfte zu imaginieren. Jede Session endet mit einer spekulativen Postkarte, die basierend auf dem Gespräch der Gruppe co-kreiert wird.

Web Preview Text EN: What happens when movement becomes a form of dialogue—not only between people, but also between human and machine? In this workshop, we will explore new ways of moving in relation to ourselves, to each other, to audiences with and without mediation by digitally generated movements and sounds.
Description EN:
How can individual movement signatures be mapped, recognised and predicted? 
How can a dancing dialogue with the HAMLET Generative AI tools: Dance Style Analysis and Generation Enabler and the Music-to-Movement Enabler lead to new ways of inhabiting and discovering our bodies through movement, of relating to each other and to the tangibly physical and intangible, intuitively intelligible latent spaces into which we are immersed? The workshop invites participants to dance dialogues with(out) AI.

—
The workshop will be documented through audio/photo/video. The documentation will be used for research and communication of the project HAMLET. Participants’s information will be processed according to GDPR. By registering, the participants consent to be documented.
Credits short:

Pilot 3 is led by ICK Dans Amsterdam, in collaboration with Centre of Excellence for Research & Innovation in Cyprus (CYENS), Aristotle University of Thessaloniki (AUTH). Pilot 4 is led by IJAD Dance, in collaboration with CYENS and The Audience Agency. Workshop coordination by Waag Futurelab, technical support by AUTH and CYENS.
Credits long: HAMLET is Horizon Europe project (Grant Agreement No 101178362). HAMLET stands for "Human-centred generative Ai fraMework for culturaL industriEs’ digital Transition (HAMLET)". In the eyes of Big Techs, creatives are users of generative AI tools. Yet in HAMLET, we take a different approach: artists and creatives are creators of AI—they closely collaborate with technologists to create AI tools that can contribute meaningfully to their practices, while addressing ethical and environmental concerns. Web Preview Text EN: In a playful creative futuring and scenario-building lab, participants will collectively map out the Linz Danubian ecosphere over the next 25 years. At the center of attention will be a special furry inhabitant—the beaver—playing the part of a primary cultural, political and technical protagonist.
Description EN: What can we learn from the transformative powers of the beaver? In this workshop, participants will experiment with creative futuring and forecasting methods to generate nuanced, multi-species scenarios that reframe the beaver from a passive wild animal to an active, technical and cultural stakeholder in landscape design and restoration. A guided process will unleash their imagination to co-create speculative worlds, culminating in a historical, yet tangible retrospective from the year 2051.
Web Preview Text DE: In einem spielerischen Labor für kreative Zukunftsgestaltung und Szenarienentwicklung entwerfen die Teilnehmer*innen gemeinsam die Linzer Donau-Ökosphäre der kommenden 25 Jahre. Im Mittelpunkt steht ein besonderer pelziger Bewohner: der Biber als zentraler kultureller, politischer und technischer Protagonist.
Description DE: Was können wir von den transformativen Kräften des Bibers lernen? In diesem Workshop erproben die Teilnehmer*innen Methoden kreativer Zukunftsgestaltung und Vorausschau, um nuancierte Multi-Spezies-Szenarien zu entwickeln. Darin wird der Biber vom passiven Wildtier zum aktiven technischen und kulturellen Akteur der Landschaftsgestaltung und Renaturierung. Ein angeleiteter Prozess setzt die Fantasie frei und mündet in eine greifbare Rückschau aus dem Jahr 2051.

Web Preview Text EN: B10d13$3L-LLM is a performative installation that reveals the often-hidden costs of Artificial Intelligence.
Description EN: B10d13$3L-LLM is a performative installation by Gökay Atabek—developed in collaboration with Jan Zuiderveld and Ritsert Mans—that shows the often-hidden costs of Artificial Intelligence. The work uses a slow, “little language model” AI agent that runs on a single microcomputer powered by DIY biodiesel. In a darkly humorous way, it reveals the materiality, energy consumption and infrastructural limits of AI.

Mit schwarzem Humor legt die Arbeit die Materialität, den Energieverbrauch und die infrastrukturellen Grenzen von KI offen.

Subtitle EN: Our future begins with clean energy
Subtitle DE: Our future begins with clean energy
Web Preview Text EN: Powerplayground is a multi-room interactive exhibition at its own venue in Linz. VR experiences, hands-on stations, guided tours and events explore energy, climate and the transition beyond fossil fuels—and invite visitors to find their own role.
Description EN: How can a high standard of living be maintained without dependence on fossil fuels? Powerplayground explores this question as a multi-room interactive exhibition at its own venue in Linz. Eight connected zones lead from energy and everyday life through the history and consequences of fossil-fuel use to climate change, renewable energy, practical solutions, education and green careers. Visitors encounter VR experiences, hands-on installations, energy visualizations, pedal-powered stations, guided tours, talks and partner projects. The exhibition connects scientific knowledge with social and political questions: Who produces and controls energy, who bears the consequences, and how can the transition become fair and achievable? It presents the energy transition not only as a technical challenge, but as a cultural transformation that needs many skills and professions.
Web Preview Text DE: Powerplayground ist eine interaktive Ausstellung mit mehreren Themenräumen an einem eigenen Standort in Linz. VR-Erlebnisse, Mitmachstationen, Führungen und Events machen Energie, Klima und den Ausstieg aus fossilen Energien greifbar – und zeigen Handlungsmöglichkeiten.
Description DE: Wie lässt sich ein hoher Lebensstandard sichern, ohne von fossiler Energie abhängig zu bleiben? Im Powerplayground stellen wir uns diese Frage im Rahmen einer interaktiven Ausstellung mit mehreren Räumen an einem eigenen Standort in Linz. Acht verbundene Themenbereiche führen von Energie und Alltag über Geschichte und Folgen fossiler Nutzung bis zu Klimawandel, erneuerbarer Energie, konkreten Lösungen, Ausbildungen und Green Jobs. Zu sehen sind VR-Erlebnisse, Mitmachinstallationen, Energievisualisierungen, pedalbetriebene Stationen, Führungen, Vorträge und Projekte von Partnerorganisationen. Die Ausstellung verbindet wissenschaftliches Wissen mit gesellschaftlichen und politischen Fragen: Wer erzeugt und kontrolliert Energie, wer trägt die Folgen und wie kann die Energiewende gerecht und umsetzbar werden? Sie zeigt die Energiewende nicht nur als technische Aufgabe, sondern als kulturelle Transformation.

Web Preview Text EN: The Johannes Kepler University Linz looks back at sixty years: six decades full of research, education, social responsibility, and the claim not just to observe change, but to shape it. The JKU MED Campus will offer a space for interdisciplinary research, artistic perspectives and social questions.
Description EN:
The future begins. But it doesn’t start from nothing. It starts with a question that we ask. With the knowledge that we store and create. With the values we defend. And with the courage to renegotiate what seems given.
 
In 2026, two anniversaries coincide that talk about the future in a special way. The Johannes Kepler University Linz looks back at sixty years: six decades full of research, education, social responsibility, and the claim not just to observe change, but to shape it. The Ars Electronica Center and the Futurelab celebrate thirty years of existence, where art, technology and society are intertwined in new ways again and again.
 
Both stories show: The future does not just start tomorrow. It started a long time ago. In auditoriums and exhibitions, in laboratories and offices, in scientific and artistic experiments, in conversations and discussions.
 
In this respect, NEGOTIATING HUMANITY – FUTURE BEGINS is more than just a festival theme. It is an invitation to understand humankind as an open question. What does humanity mean in times in which machines keep learning, systems take decisions and realities can be simulated? What role do science, art and education play, when technologies are developing faster than our social agreements? And how is it possible to understand progress not only as acceleration, but as responsibility?
 
These questions are a matter at the heart of the JKU. As a university, we do not just wait for the future. We are part of its genesis. We research technologies that change our world. We educate people who will go on to shape this world. And we take responsibility for ensuring that knowledge is not only efficient, but also accessible, critical, democratic and human.
 
For all these reasons, JKU is sending a strong signal by not only hosting the Ars Electronica Festival 2026, but also by offering an active resonance chamber. The JKU MED Campus will offer a space for interdisciplinary research, artistic perspectives and social questions. This clearly shows that the human must not disappear even though technology progresses. Humans must continue to be the benchmark.
 
This approach is also demonstrated by joint projects that are realized by the JKU Linz Institute of Technology (LIT) through a special call. JKU scientists exchange inspiring ideas with locally and internationally renowned artists to create a platform to discuss and experience research at the intersection with art in a playful manner. This is not just about presenting scientific results, but about shifting perspectives. Artificial Intelligence projects, exoskeletons, algorithms, robotics, gaming cultures, radicalization, digital power structures or democratic futures all show that art and science are not mere decoration, but rather a method to shed a different light on complex questions—as the first exhibition of the Art x Science School for Transformation will demonstrate.
 
On top of that, the JKUniverse will open a space for the past, present and future together. A time capsule will not symbolize the memories, but function as a tool for participation: Which questions do we take with us? Which answers need to be renewed? Which visions of the future do we want to pass on?
 
This is exactly the power of knowledge transfer in the center of society: It doesn’t make the future abstract, but rather something that can be experienced, questioned and touched. It shows that humanity is more than a nostalgic counterpart of technology; it is an active practice. This is also proven by one of the highlights of Ars Electronica 2026, where the JKU Linz Faculty of Medicine opens the medSPACE, the virtual auditorium, physics laboratories and more to offer insights into transdisciplinary research at the interface of medicine and technology.
 
Knowledge creates a practice of listening, doubting, researching and designing. That is why the festival also offers the JKU a mirror that shows what it means to be a university in times when knowledge alone is insufficient. What it means to prepare young people not just for a career, but for taking responsibility. What it means when innovation is not just possible, but useful.
 
The answers are not provided by individual projects, individual technologies or ready-made visions. The answers are a result of negotiations. Of encounters between art and science. Between past and future. Between research and society. Between all the things we can do and the things we want to do.
 
The future begins now. And it starts where we have the courage to negotiate it together.

Stefan Koch (AT) / Rector Johannes Kepler University Linz (AT)
Web Preview Text DE: Die Johannes Kepler Universität Linz blickt auf 60 Jahre zurück: auf sechs Jahrzehnte Forschung, Lehre, gesellschaftliche Verantwortung und den Anspruch, Wandel nicht nur zu beobachten, sondern mitzugestalten. Am JKU MED Campus treffen interdisziplinäre Forschung, künstlerische Perspektiven und gesellschaftliche Fragen aufeinander.
Description DE:
Die Zukunft beginnt. Aber sie beginnt nicht aus dem Nichts. Sie beginnt mit den Fragen, die wir stellen. Mit dem Wissen, das wir bewahren und neu schaffen. Mit den Werten, die wir verteidigen. Und mit dem Mut, das, was selbstverständlich scheint, immer wieder neu zu verhandeln.

Im Jahr 2026 begegnen sich zwei Jubiläen, die auf besondere Weise von Zukunft erzählen. Die Johannes Kepler Universität Linz blickt auf 60 Jahre zurück: auf sechs Jahrzehnte Forschung, Lehre, gesellschaftliche Verantwortung und den Anspruch, Wandel nicht nur zu beobachten, sondern mitzugestalten. Das Ars Electronica Center und das Futurelab feiern ihr 30-jähriges Bestehen, in dem Kunst, Technologie und Gesellschaft immer wieder in neue Beziehungen gesetzt werden.

Beide Geschichten zeigen: Die Zukunft beginnt nicht erst morgen. Sie hat längst begonnen. In Hörsälen und Ausstellungen, in Laboren und Büros, in wissenschaftlichen und künstlerischen Experimenten, in Gesprächen und Diskussionen.

NEGOTIATING HUMANITY – FUTURE BEGINS ist daher mehr als ein Festivalthema. Es ist eine Einladung, das Menschsein selbst als offene Frage zu verstehen. Was bedeutet Humanität in einer Zeit, in der Maschinen lernen, Systeme entscheiden und Wirklichkeiten simuliert werden? Welche Rolle spielen Wissenschaft, Kunst und Bildung, wenn technologische Möglichkeiten schneller wachsen als unsere gesellschaftlichen Vereinbarungen? Und wie gelingt es, Fortschritt nicht nur als Beschleunigung, sondern als Verantwortung zu denken?

Für die JKU Linz sind diese Fragen zentral. Als Universität warten wir nicht auf die Zukunft. Wir sind Teil ihrer Entstehung. Wir forschen an Technologien, die unsere Welt verändern. Wir bilden Menschen aus, die diese Welt gestalten werden. Und wir tragen Verantwortung dafür, dass Wissen nicht nur leistungsfähig, sondern auch zugänglich, kritisch, demokratisch und menschlich bleibt.

Deshalb ist es ein starkes Zeichen, dass die JKU Linz beim Ars Electronica Festival 2026 nicht nur Gastgeberin, sondern auch aktiver Resonanzraum ist. Am JKU MED Campus treffen interdisziplinäre Forschung, künstlerische Perspektiven und gesellschaftliche Fragen aufeinander. Hier wird besonders deutlich: Der Mensch darf im technologischen Fortschritt nicht verschwinden. Er muss sein Maßstab bleiben.

Diese Haltung zeigt sich auch in den gemeinsamen Projekten, die im Zuge des Sonder-Calls des JKU Linz Institute of Technology (LIT) realisiert werden. Wissenschaftler*innen der JKU Linz treten hier mit lokalen und international bekannten Künstler*innen in einen inspirierenden Austausch, um Forschung an der Schnittstelle zur Kunst erfahrbar und spielerisch diskutierbar zu machen. Dabei werden nicht einfach wissenschaftliche Ergebnisse präsentiert, sondern Perspektiven verschoben. Projekte zu Künstlicher Intelligenz, Exoskeletten, Algorithmen, Robotik, Gaming-Kulturen, Radikalisierung, digitalen Machtstrukturen oder demokratischen Zukünften zeigen, dass Art & Science kein dekorativer Zusatz ist. Es ist eine Methode, um komplexe Fragen anders sichtbar zu machen, wie auch die erstmalige Ausstellung der Art x Science School for Transformation zeigen wird.

Weiters öffnet das JKUniverse einen Raum, in dem Vergangenheit, Gegenwart und Zukunft miteinander ins Gespräch kommen. Eine Zeitkapsel wird dabei nicht nur zum Symbol des Erinnerns, sondern zum Werkzeug der Beteiligung: Welche Fragen nehmen wir mit? Welche Antworten müssen wir erneuern? Welche Zukunftsbilder wollen wir weitergeben?

Genau darin liegt die Kraft der Wissenschaftsvermittlung mitten in der Gesellschaft: Sie macht Zukunft nicht abstrakt. Sie macht sie begreifbar, befragbar, erfahrbar. Sie zeigt, dass Menschlichkeit kein nostalgischer Gegenbegriff zur Technologie ist, sondern eine aktive Praxis. Das beweist auch eines der Highlights beim Ars Electronica 2026, bei dem die Medizinische Fakultät der JKU Linz vom JKU medSPACE, dem virtuellen Hörsaal, bis zu den physischen Laboren Einblicke in die transdisziplinäre Forschung an der Schnittstelle von Medizin und Technik gibt.

Wissen schaffen ist eine Praxis des Zuhörens, des Zweifelns, des Forschens, des Gestaltens. Für die JKU Linz ist dieses Festival daher auch ein Blick in den Spiegel. Was heißt es, Universität in einer Zeit zu sein, in der Wissen allein nicht genügt? Was heißt es, junge Menschen nicht nur für Berufe, sondern für Verantwortung vorzubereiten? Was heißt es, Innovation nicht nur möglich, sondern sinnvoll zu machen?

Die Antwort liegt nicht in einem einzigen Projekt, nicht in einer einzelnen Technologie, nicht in einer fertigen Vision. Sie liegt im gemeinsamen Verhandeln. In der Begegnung zwischen Kunst und Wissenschaft. Zwischen Vergangenheit und Zukunft. Zwischen Forschung und Gesellschaft. Zwischen dem, was wir können, und dem, was wir wollen.

Die Zukunft beginnt jetzt. Und sie beginnt dort, wo wir den Mut haben, sie gemeinsam zu verhandeln.

Stefan Koch (AT) / Rektor Johannes Kepler University Linz (AT)

Web Preview Text EN: Negotiating with Water is a conference programme dedicated to our water imaginaries, and their legal and geopolitical realities and possibilities. The day examines our fraught relation to water that has led to the multiple crises of our time, and suggests its rerouting towards a more fluid one in which we continuously negotiate with others, most importantly, with water itself.
Description EN:
Negotiating with Water is a conference programme dedicated to our water imaginaries, and their legal and geopolitical realities and possibilities. The day frames water as a symptom of the socio-political context and a witness to different forms of human activities. Through the gaze of capital, water is a resource, a commodity we negotiate the rights to; at the same time, water carries traces of military, logistic or commercial activity.  
Current water imaginaries have led to our thirsty, expansion-driven culture becoming the site of multiple water-related crises—from the persistent freshwater crisis to more recent geopolitical dynamics that have highlighted the importance of bodies of water for global trade and military action.   
To frame water as a product of socio-political and cultural imaginaries is to also reframe water crises as cultural. It means to ask not only what water imaginaries might be possible under different conditions, but also what innovation and legal frameworks they would allow; it means breaking with the history of water told only in scientific, techno-managerial or colonial terms. 
Throughout the conference day, artists, theorists, indigenous thinkers and legal experts complicate the existing notion of water and think with water to reimagine hydro-social relations across different scales. The conference examines our fraught relation to water that has led to the multiple crises of our time and suggests its rerouting towards a more fluid one in which we continuously negotiate with others, and most importantly, with water itself.

Name EN: Water through a Legal Lens: From Private Commodity to the Heritage of Mankind
Web Preview Text EN: Stefano Burchi's talk unpacks the evolving legal conceptions of (fresh)water, from water as a private commodity to water as public property regulated by nation-states through national water laws, all the way to the water of boundary rivers, lakes and aquifers framed in treaties and agreements between multiple nation-states.
Description EN:
Stefano Burchi's talk unpacks the evolving legal conceptions of (fresh)water, from water as a private commodity to water as public property regulated by nation-states through national water laws, all the way to the water of boundary rivers, lakes and aquifers framed in treaties and agreements between multiple nation-states. These legal conceptions illustrate how nation-states and, more broadly, humans and societies relate to water.

Against this backdrop, the talk raises questions about the possibilities to upscale the legal discourse about water from the level of individuals, communities and nation-states acting in their self-interest to a global level, where water is regarded as the heritage of mankind, governed by norms that appeal universally and (ideally) emanate from—and are administered by—a supranational authority.

Web Preview Text EN: A giant, gravity-powered contraption that wakes Joseph, lifts him from bed, washes his face, dresses him and shoves him face-first into a croissant—built and filmed live in front of a public audience.
Description EN: The creator of the YouTube channel Joseph’s Machines invites audiences behind the scenes to witness the creation of his viral videos. Watch in real time as he builds and films his biggest contraption yet: a human-scale morning routine machine where the performer is hoisted out of bed and propelled down a conveyor belt to be mechanically dressed and fed. In a society obsessed with productivity, the project is a joyful rebellion. By making simple tasks absurdly complicated, it celebrates the beauty of deliberate inefficiency and asks how to reclaim joy in a hyper-optimized world. The installation explores the art of failure, and the importance of play in the creation process. Success is fundamentally built on a willingness to experiment, get things wrong and try again.
Web Preview Text DE: Eine gigantische, von der Schwerkraft angetriebene Konstruktion, die Joseph aufweckt, ihn aus dem Bett hebt, sein Gesicht wäscht, ihn anzieht und ihn mit dem Gesicht voran in ein Croissant schubst – live vor Publikum gebaut und gefilmt.
Description DE: Der Schöpfer des YouTube-Kanals Joseph’s Machines lädt Besucher*innen dazu ein, einen Blick hinter die Kulissen zu werfen und die Entstehung seiner viralen Videos live zu erleben. In Echtzeit baut und filmt er hier seine bisher größte Konstruktion: eine menschengroße Morgenroutine-Maschine, die den Performer aus dem Bett hebt und über ein Förderband transportiert um ihn mechanisch anzuziehen und zu füttern. In einer Gesellschaft, die von Produktivität besessen ist, versteht sich das Projekt als freudvolle Rebellion. Indem es einfache Aufgaben absurd verkompliziert, feiert es die Schönheit bewusster Ineffizienz und stellt die Frage, wie sich Freude in einer hyperoptimierten Welt zurückgewinnen lässt. Die Installation erkundet die Kunst des Scheiterns und die Bedeutung des Spiels im kreativen Prozess. Denn Erfolg basiert letztlich auf der Bereitschaft, zu experimentieren, Fehler zu machen und es immer wieder aufs Neue zu versuchen.

Artists: Adrien Lucca (FR/BE), Ali Aiman Raza (IN/FR), Colas Schretter (BE), Marko Ilić (SI)
Web Preview Text EN: How does the same garden appear to another species? Under custom LED light, leaves darken and flowers become strikingly bright, offering a scientifically informed translation of the elephant hawkmoth’s colour vision and a glimpse of a perceptual world normally invisible to humans.
Description EN: The installation presents a living garden of plants and flowers beneath a custom, computer-controlled LED system. At regular intervals, the light turns bluish and the colors of the garden change completely: green foliage becomes brown or dark, while flowers appear brighter and stand out more strongly from the background. The transformation evokes how the elephant hawkmoth Deilephila elpenor may perceive the same plants through a color vision adapted to finding flowers among leaves. Based on scientific research, the work offers an informed translation rather than a claim to reproduce exactly what the animal sees. It invites the audience to experience a simple but profound idea: the same world can look entirely different to another living being. By combining colour science, sensory ecology and contemporary art, the project makes an otherwise inaccessible perceptual world temporarily visible to human eyes.
Web Preview Text DE: Wie sieht derselbe Garten aus der Perspektive einer anderen Spezies aus? Unter speziell entwickeltem LED-Licht verdunkeln sich Blätter, während Blüten in auffälliger Helligkeit erstrahlen. So entsteht eine wissenschaftlich fundierte Übersetzung des Farbsehens des Mittleren Weinschwärmers – und ein Einblick in eine Wahrnehmungswelt, die für den Menschen normalerweise unsichtbar bleibt.
Description DE: Dieselbe Landschaft kann je nachdem, wer sie betrachtet, völlig unterschiedlich aussehen. Parallel World ist das Ergebnis einer langjährigen Zusammenarbeit zwischen Kunst, Farbwissenschaft, Biologie, Gartenbau und Ingenieurwesen. Das Projekt untersucht, wie der Nachtfalter Deilephila elpenor blühende Pflanzen bei nahezu vollständiger Dunkelheit wahrnimmt. Besucher*innen begegnen einem Garten aus Pflanzen und Blüten, der unter einem computergesteuerten LED-System gedeiht. In regelmäßigen Abständen verschiebt sich das Licht ins Blaue, und die Farben des Gartens verändern sich grundlegend: Grünes Blattwerk erscheint braun oder dunkel, während die Blüten heller hervortreten und sich deutlich von ihrer Umgebung abheben. Statt die Wahrnehmung des Insekts nachzubilden, übersetzt die Installation auf fundierte Weise seine sensorische Ökologie und zeigt, wie künstliches Licht die ökologische Kommunikation zwischen Bestäubern und Pflanzen verändert. Die Arbeit bringt wissenschaftliche Forschung in direkten Dialog mit lebendiger Materie und macht so die ökologischen Folgen der Lichtverschmutzung durch eine subtile, aber tiefgreifende Transformation des Gartens unmittelbar erfahrbar.

Web Preview Text EN: Our democracies and constitutions rest on foundations that were originally laid in a very different world. In this participatory workshop, IG Demokratie invites participants to explore the roots of the current crisis of democracy.
Description EN: Our democracies and constitutions rest on foundations that were originally laid in a very different world. As societies confront multiple, interconnected crises, many are asking whether our political systems are still equipped to meet today’s challenges. In this participatory workshop, IG Demokratie invites participants to explore the roots of the current crisis of democracy. What lies at its core? Political parties? Patriarchal structures? Escalating techno-capitalism? Or something else entirely? Through collective reflection and discussion, this workshop examines how political structures might be dismantled, redesigned and renewed. After all, the political system belongs to us all—and so does the opportunity to shape its future.
Web Preview Text DE: Unsere Demokratien und Verfassungen beruhen auf Grundlagen, die ursprünglich in einer ganz anderen Welt geschaffen wurden. In diesem partizipativen Workshop lädt die IG Demokratie die Teilnehmer*innen ein, den Wurzeln der aktuellen Krise der Demokratie nachzugehen.
Description DE: Unsere Demokratien und Verfassungen beruhen auf Grundlagen, die ursprünglich in einer ganz anderen Welt geschaffen wurden. Während Gesellschaften mit vielfältigen, miteinander verflochtenen Krisen konfrontiert sind, fragen sich viele, ob unsere politischen Systeme den heutigen Herausforderungen noch gewachsen sind. In diesem partizipativen Workshop lädt die IG Demokratie die Teilnehmer*innen ein, den Wurzeln der aktuellen Krise der Demokratie nachzugehen. Was ist ihr Kern? Politische Parteien? Patriarchale Strukturen? Eskalierender Techno-Kapitalismus? Oder etwas ganz anderes? Im gemeinsamen Nachdenken und Diskutieren untersucht der Workshop, wie politische Strukturen aufgebrochen, neu gestaltet und erneuert werden können. Denn das politische System gehört uns allen – ebenso wie die Möglichkeit, seine Zukunft zu gestalten.

Name EN: Next Singularity, the Intelligence of Life

Web Preview Text EN: AI will become increasingly intelligent. But the future still depends on the intelligence of life itself.
Description EN: For nearly 50 years, artist Yoichiro Kawaguchi has utilized his original “Growth Model” to explore biological forms and evolution through computer-generated art, blending natural mathematics with advanced technology. His work, drawing inspiration from the Cambrian explosion, argues that AI should be a creative partner for discovering human singularity rather than a tool for producing standardized, mediocre content.

Description DE: Seit fast 50 Jahren nutzt der Künstler Yoichiro Kawaguchi sein selbst entwickeltes “Growth Model”, um mithilfe computergenerierter Kunst biologische Formen und Evolution zu erforschen und dabei natürliche Mathematik mit moderner Technologie zu verbinden. Inspiriert von der kambrischen Explosion vertritt er die These, dass KI nicht zur Produktion standardisierter, mittelmäßiger Inhalte dienen soll, sondern als kreative Partnerin, mit der sich die Einzigartigkeit des Menschen neu entdecken lässt.

Name EN: AI for Social Impact – Negotiating Humanity in Times of Crisis
Subtitle EN: Negotiating Humanity in Times of Crisis
Subtitle DE: Negotiating Humanity in Times of Crisis
Web Preview Text EN: Initiated in collaboration with CARE Austria, this conference explores how Artificial Intelligence can contribute to addressing humanitarian, social and environmental challenges. Against the backdrop of growing crises, it highlights initiatives that use AI to improve access to healthcare, education, information, humanitarian services and food security, while strengthening the agency of vulnerable communities.
Description EN:
Initiated in collaboration with CARE Austria, this conference explores how Artificial Intelligence can contribute to addressing humanitarian, social, and environmental challenges. Marking CARE Austria’s 80th anniversary, it builds on the momentum of the inaugural AI for Social Impact Award, presented this year as part of the Prix Ars Electronica, and extends its central question into a broader public conversation: how can AI be developed and deployed to strengthen humanitarian action in a rapidly changing world?

Against the backdrop of growing crises, armed conflicts, displacement, widening inequalities and the accelerating impacts of climate change, the conference brings together practitioners, researchers, artists and experts working across humanitarian action and technology to examine both the opportunities and the limitations of AI. It highlights initiatives that use AI to improve access to healthcare, education, information, humanitarian services and food security, while strengthening the agency of vulnerable communities. Rather than celebrating technology for its own sake, these projects demonstrate how AI can amplify human expertise, support local capacities and address concrete humanitarian needs in contexts where resources are scarce and challenges are acute.

At the same time, the conference critically examines the tensions between rising humanitarian needs and the growing influence of AI-driven systems. Under what conditions can AI create meaningful social impact? What roles do transparency, accountability, data governance and local knowledge play? And how can humanitarian organizations harness the potential of AI without becoming increasingly dependent on the infrastructures, business models and services of a small number of global technology providers?

Rather than treating AI as an end in itself, the conference approaches it as a subject of social negotiation—one that requires democratic oversight, ethical responsibility and sustained collaboration across disciplines and sectors. From this perspective, the conference culminates in a call to action for the humanitarian sector: not merely to adopt AI, but to actively shape its development and governance, ensuring that technological innovation remains grounded in humanitarian principles, local realities and the rights of the communities it is intended to support.
Funding Line: This symposium is curated in partnership with CARE Austria's and made possible through CC Real's generous support.

Web Preview Text EN: Andrea Barschdorf-Hager, CEO of CARE Austria and Gerfried Stocker, Artistic Director of Ars Electronica, open the day by reflecting on the collaboration between the two organizations and the shared questions that bring the worlds of humanitarian action, art, technology and innovation together.
Description EN:
Andrea Barschdorf-Hager, CEO of CARE Austria and Gerfried Stocker, Artistic Director of Ars Electronica, open the day by reflecting on the collaboration between the two organizations and the shared questions that bring the worlds of humanitarian action, art, technology and innovation together.

Connecting to this year’s Ars Electronica Festival theme, NEGOTIATING HUMANITY they introduce the central questions of the day: How is our understanding of humanity changing in an age increasingly shaped by Artificial Intelligence? Who benefits from technological progress—and who risks being left behind? Their opening remarks set the stage for a day of exchange on how AI can contribute to social impact while keeping human needs, dignity and agency at its core.
Funding Line: This symposium is curated in partnership with CARE Austria's and made possible through CC Real's generous support.

Description EN: Hito Steyerl’s opening keynote sets the conceptual framework for AI for Social Impact – Negotiating Humanity in Times of Crisis. Drawing on her artistic and theoretical practice, she examines the shifting relationships between technology, power, human experience and collective agency. Connecting her critical engagement with digital technologies to questions of participation and social responsibility, she explores how AI is reshaping our understanding of humanity and what new forms of solidarity and collective action might emerge in response. She invites us to approach AI not simply as a technological development, but as a cultural, political and social force that challenges us to reconsider what it means to be human in times of crisis.

Name EN: One in seven: Austria 1946, Uganda 2026—who gets to be a person in a crisis?
Web Preview Text EN: This keynote explores how visibility, data and global attention shape our understanding of humanitarian crises and asks what this means as Artificial Intelligence becomes increasingly influential in humanitarian and social impact work.
Description EN:
Not all crises are seen equally—and neither are the people living through them. This keynote explores how visibility, data and global attention shape our understanding of humanitarian crises and asks what this means as Artificial Intelligence becomes increasingly influential in humanitarian and social impact work.

Beginning with the history of the CARE Package in post-war Austria, the keynote connects past and present experiences of crisis and reflects on the agency of those affected. Drawing on contemporary examples, including Sudan and Ukraine, it asks whether AI systems—often unintentionally—may understand some crises better than others because some people, places and realities are more visible in the data on which they rely.

At its heart is a fundamental question: How can AI support people in crisis without overlooking those it cannot easily see? The keynote concludes with questions that open the conversation for the fireside chat that follows.
Funding Line: This symposium is curated in partnership with CARE Austria's and made possible through CC Real's generous support.

Who gets to shape the future of Artificial Intelligence—and whose voices risk being left out?

Bringing together perspectives from technology and humanitarian practice, this conversation explores how AI can be developed in ways that are equitable, inclusive and accountable. Archana Prasad, founder of http://gooey.ai/, brings the perspective of a technologist and entrepreneur working at the intersection of AI and social impact, while Jerry Tuan, CEO of CARE USA, contributes insights from global humanitarian practice. The conversation is moderated by Andrea Barschdorf-Hager.

Together, they discuss how power and responsibility are shared between those who build AI, the institutions that deploy it, and the communities affected by it. The session asks what it takes to ensure that a broader range of voices can meaningfully participate in shaping the future of AI.

Name EN: AI for Social Impact Award: Insights from the Jury & Introduction to the Initiative
Web Preview Text EN: How can Artificial Intelligence contribute to meaningful social change—and what does it take for an AI-driven project to create impact that is not only innovative, but also responsible, inclusive and sustainable?
Description EN:
How can Artificial Intelligence contribute to meaningful social change—and what does it take for an AI-driven project to create impact that is not only innovative, but also responsible, inclusive and sustainable?

This session introduces the AI for Social Impact Award, its vision, objectives and selection process. The award seeks to recognize initiatives that use AI to address pressing social and humanitarian challenges while placing people, communities and ethical responsibility at the center of technological development.

Drawing on their experience as part of the jury process, Andrea and Gerfried share key observations from the submitted projects and offer insights into the questions that shaped the selection. What distinguishes technological innovation from meaningful social impact? How can impact be assessed across very different cultural, social and humanitarian contexts? And what role do accessibility, community involvement, scalability and ethical design play in evaluating AI for social good?

Looking across the submissions, the session also highlights emerging trends, recurring challenges and new opportunities in the field. It provides a broader perspective on how AI is currently being used for social impact around the world—and sets the stage for the presentation of the winning initiatives that follows.
Funding Line: This symposium is curated in partnership with CARE Austria and made possible through CC Real's generous support.

Name EN: AI for Social Impact Award: The award winning projects
Artists: Eniola Benson (NG), Shadi Henchiri (TN), Oluwaseun Kayode (NG), Esther Kimani (KE), Rafael Lozano-Hemmer (MX)
Web Preview Text EN: What does it look like when Artificial Intelligence is designed not simply to innovate, but to respond to real social and humanitarian needs?
Description EN:
What does it look like when Artificial Intelligence is designed not simply to innovate, but to respond to real social and humanitarian needs?

This session presents the five winning initiatives of the AI for Social Impact Initiative, showcasing projects that combine technological innovation with measurable social impact, ethical design and meaningful engagement with the communities they aim to serve. Spanning education, agriculture, historical justice, migrant health and maternal care, the projects demonstrate very different ways in which AI can become a tool for social change.

The three Awards of Distinction highlight this diversity of approaches. Oluwaseun Kayode and the Schoolinka Team present an AI-powered tool supporting teachers in Nigeria by assessing competencies and providing individualized feedback for professional development. Esther Kimani and Farmer Lifeline demonstrate how solar-powered AI can help smallholder farmers detect crop diseases and pests, respond to climate risks and strengthen food security. Rafael Lozano-Hemmer and the Antimetric Institute explore a very different application with Global Level of Confidence, using facial recognition technology in the context of Argentina’s disappeared to address questions of memory, identity, human rights and justice.

The two Grand Prize winners focus on access to healthcare in underserved and vulnerable communities. Shadi Henchiri’s Afiya AI uses a WhatsApp-based AI system to help migrants navigate complex healthcare systems and access essential health information and services. Eniola Benson and HelpMum use AI-powered tools to support maternal and infant health, from identifying high-risk pregnancies to improving vaccination access and providing health guidance through widely accessible digital channels.

Together, these five initiatives invite us to look beyond AI as a technology in itself and consider the contexts in which it operates: Who does it serve? What problem does it address? How accessible is it to the people who need it most? And how can technological innovation translate into meaningful and lasting social impact?

The session offers an opportunity to meet the people behind the winning projects and gain insight into how their ideas emerged, how they work in practice and what they can teach us about developing AI that responds to human and societal needs.
Funding Line: This symposium is curated in partnership with CARE Austria and made possible through CC Real's generous support.

Artists: Eniola Benson (NG), Shadi Henchiri (TN), Milagros Miceli (AR), Vivian Tabeth (EG) moderated by Reshma Khan (KE)
Web Preview Text EN: Bringing the symposium to a close, this panel explores what it means to keep humanity at the center of Artificial Intelligence in humanitarian action.
Description EN:
Bringing the symposium to a close, this panel explores what it means to keep humanity at the center of Artificial Intelligence in humanitarian action. It brings together perspectives from AI innovation, humanitarian practice, critical data studies and community-centered implementation to examine both the potential and the tensions that arise when AI is developed and deployed in contexts of vulnerability and crisis.

The discussion features Eniola Benson and Shadi Henchiri, Grand Prize winners of the AI for Social Impact Initiative, who bring insights from developing AI solutions with and for vulnerable communities; Milagros Miceli, an expert in data ethics and the politics of AI and data infrastructures; and Vivian Thabet, CEO of CARE Egypt, who contributes a humanitarian and organizational perspective. The conversation is moderated by Reshma Khan.

Moving beyond the question of what AI can do, the panel asks what responsible, equitable and genuinely human-centered AI should look like. What principles should guide its development? What trade-offs and limitations must we be willing to acknowledge? And how can communities affected by these technologies have a meaningful role in shaping them?

Each panelist will bring one concrete commitment or principle to the discussion, culminating in a collective Call to Action—not as a final consensus, but as a set of complementary perspectives and commitments for more responsible, equitable and community-driven innovation in humanitarian AI.
Funding Line: This symposium is curated in partnership with CARE Austria and made possible through CC Real's generous support.

Name EN: Contested Futures – Europe Negotiating Power, Machine, Labour
Artists: Curated by Francesca Bria and José Luis de Vicente
Subtitle EN: A one-day forum by the Archipelago of Possible Futures and the S+T+ARTS Day 2026
Web Preview Text EN: If being human has always been a process of negotiation, then this day asks the following question: How does Europe negotiate its future, when so much of that future is now built into the machines, the infrastructures of modern power, underpinning our collective life?
Description EN:
If being human has always been a process of negotiation, then this day asks the following question: How does Europe negotiate its future, when so much of that future is now built into the machines, the infrastructures of modern power, underpinning our collective life?

It is not a settled question. It is not a friendly one. The same drive for digital sovereignty can also build public infrastructure held in common—or a militarized arsenal dressed in the aesthetics of a new authoritarianism. The future is contested. Europe has to choose, out in the open.

So this is not a conference. It is an archipelago, a set of connected conversations, each a constellation of another possible Europe. Together they trace the architectures of power behind the machine: the hidden human labor that trains AI; the geopolitics of automated conflict; the diplomacy of the tech stack, of space and cyberspace; the science inventing the next world; and the journalism, campaigns and worker conscience rising to confront unchecked technological power.

Art runs through all of it, not as ornament, but as infrastructure for negotiation: making conflict possible, making visible what power erases, holding open the space where contested truths can be named. Because naming is already an intervention. And because a “sovereign” European way must mean not only what we build, but what we refuse to build: computing within limits to preserve collective rights on a living planet.
The day does not seek consensus. It seeks the harder, more human thing: the capacity for self-transformation. To hold contradiction. To negotiate legitimate conflicts rather than settle them by force. To imagine and draw a collective future here, deliberately, together.

We do not need less technology. We need better reasons to build it, and the courage to build it on our own terms: for our labor, our planet and a life in common.
